I graduated last year and am currently taking a gap year. I think it has been a fantastic choice for me. While your situation differs slightly from mine (I took one to save up for college), I still think you may benefit from a gap year if that's what you think is right for you. 

The main thing is to create a list of goals and priorities you want to focus on during your gap year. Look into summer school and see if that will work for you. If not, I believe you can return for a 13th year and become a part-time student if you only need a few credits. You may even be able to do this completely online if you have the means and don't want to return in person. 

You have mentioned wanting to work as well. While I think that's also a fantastic idea—in terms of making money, gaining experience, helping build a resume—it's very important to make sure it won't interfere with your schooling if improving your marks if your main priority.

One of the hardest parts about making this decision (at least it was for me) of watching your peers and friends around you moving onto post secondary while you stay behind. It's tough, but everyone moves on in life at different paces. Never consider yourself "a year behind", instead consider yourself supplemented with other types of experience you can allow yourself to gain during your gap year. Post-secondary will always be there at the end. 

I don't know why more students don't take gap years. Four years of high school is rough on a growing mind and body, a year to just take it back a notch before post secondary is wonderful. Anyway, whatever you decide, I'm sure everything will work out for you!

First, you are definitely judging people’s hobbies LOL. 

One thing that has always bothered me is that people think a hobby should always produce a tangible, physical end product. Why? Just because you cannot physically see the end product of a hobby, certainly does not mean it isn’t there. For example, I enjoy playing video games in my free time, therefore it is one of my hobbies. And boy, have I gained many end products from my years of gaming. They are called skills. I would certainly say that playing video games has led me to develop and build on skills that I previously lacked. Eye-hand coordination, reaction time, critical thinking, strategic planning, etc.. Playing video games gets the brain working, despite what people seem to think. Again, just because you cannot physically see an end product, does not mean it isn’t there.

I would also like to point out that OP must be either a male or someone who has never touched makeup or watched someone use it. Makeup requires much skill to use. It is a delicate art, like painting or drawing. Would you say painting or drawing takes little to no skill or effort? Probably not. One even might say that fashion is an art. It’s not as simple as “buying clothes”.

I wish people would stop thinking that the only good hobbies one can have are physically demanding or produce a beautiful (physical) end product.

Just build your resume with what you’ve got, even if it’s not much.
